column1: The Lifeways of Hunter-Gatherers: The Foraging Spectrum|1995|10|0||9,9,8,9,8,9,7,9,7,8|Robert L. Kelly|Comparative synthesis explains variation in foraging, mobility, technology, exchange and social organization. Its main value is explanatory rather than procedural specialist training. Ecology is central, so T11 applies. The 2013 preface identifies this as a revised edition of the 1995 book; revised title does not reset publication age. Contents and preface inspected, not the full text. https://assets.cambridge.org/97811070/24878/frontmatter/9781107024878_frontmatter.pdf

Self Rule: A Cultural History of American Democracy|1995|10|10||8,8,7,7,7,9,6,9,8,8|Robert H. Wiebe|Connects individualism, collective organization and popular political participation across American history. The tension between personal autonomy and majority rule is transferable, but the national political narrative is a weak thematic fit. Historical cases add distinctions; no full-text density claim. https://openlibrary.org/books/OL1108622M/Self-rule

The Wars For Asia, 1911-1949|2012|0|10|1949|9,9,8,8,8,9,8,9,8,8|S. C. M. Paine|Relates Chinese civil conflict, Japanese expansion and the wider international war. Multiple interacting wars show how local and grand strategy conflict. Distinct political objectives and logistical constraints justify the detailed chronology; military power remains central.

The African Colonial State in Comparative Perspective|1994|0|10|1990|9,9,8,8,8,9,7,9,7,8|Crawford Young|Compares colonial state forms and their institutional legacies rather than explaining outcomes through one national story. Administrative extraction, coercion and legitimacy supply transferable mechanisms. Political institutions dominate; endpoint 1990 approximates the postcolonial developments used to assess the legacy.

Economics and Empire, 1830-1914|1973|0|10|1914|9,9,8,8,8,9,8,9,7,8|D. K. Fieldhouse|Tests economic explanations of imperial expansion against political and local factors. Distinguishing motives from outcomes and comparing cases strengthens causal discipline. Trade and finance are connected to state action, but imperial power is the organizing subject. https://openlibrary.org/authors/OL232887A/D._K._Fieldhouse

Making the Unipolar Moment: U.S. Foreign Policy and the Rise of the Post-Cold War Order|2016|10|10|1991|8,9,8,8,8,9,8,9,8,8|Hal Brands|Explains the interaction of economic change, diplomacy, ideology and strategic choices in the rise of American predominance. It offers reusable questions about adapting to structural change, with limits from a U.S.-centered view. Main period ends with the Cold War.

Governing the Market: Economic Theory and the Role of Government in East Asian Industrialization|1990|0|0|1988|9,10,9,9,8,9,9,9,7,8|Robert Wade|Examines industrial learning, investment coordination and government-market interaction in East Asian development. Institutional and production detail tests abstract policy claims. Industrialization leads; politics is a causal layer. Endpoint 1988 approximates the empirical period behind the original study.

Democracies Divided|2019|0|10||8,8,8,8,8,8,7,9,8,8|Thomas Carothers; Andrew O'Donohue (editors)|Comparative studies examine how polarization escalates and how institutions or leaders may contain it. Different country cases add boundary conditions, although recent histories cannot establish durable predictions. Policy analysis is not itself partisan mobilization.

Government’s End|1994|10|10||7,8,8,8,7,8,7,8,8,8|Jonathan Rauch|Explains how organized interests and accumulated commitments constrain government adaptation. The mechanism transfers beyond Washington, but selective examples and a strong organizing thesis require caution. The publisher identifies this as a later edition of Demosclerosis, so 1994 is retained as the original year. https://www.hachettebookgroup.com/titles/jon-rauch/governments-end/9781891620492/

The Fate of Rome: Climate, Disease, and the End of An Empire|2017|10|10|700|7,9,7,8,8,8,6,9,8,8|Kyle Harper|Combines political history with climate and disease evidence to explain Roman vulnerability. The synthesis adds important constraints, but attributing particular political outcomes to reconstructed environmental shocks remains uncertain. Disease, environment and imperial power incur both deductions; endpoint 700 approximates the late-antique scope.

Secular Cycles|2009|0|10||7,9,9,9,8,9,8,9,7,8|Peter Turchin; Sergey A. Nefedov|Compares population, elite competition, fiscal pressure and political instability in agrarian societies. Quantitative models are used to explain historical mechanisms, not primarily teach a technical curriculum. Sparse measurements, selection of cases and parameter choices limit predictive confidence. Different cycles contribute comparisons rather than repeated anecdotes.

Imperial Tragedy|2019|10|10|568|9,8,7,8,8,9,7,9,8,8|Michael Kulikowski|Explains Roman fragmentation through political competition, military structures and regional decisions. Context challenges a simple inevitable-collapse narrative, though the Roman institutional setting limits transfer. British title of the same work published in the U.S. as The Tragedy of Empire. https://www.everand.com/book/443186513/The-Tragedy-of-Empire-From-Constantine-to-the-Destruction-of-Roman-Italy

Imperial Triumph|2016|10|10|363|9,8,7,8,8,9,7,9,8,8|Michael Kulikowski|Explains how the Roman Empire maintained power despite succession crises and external pressures. Institutional adaptation and integration provide mechanisms beyond emperor biographies. Roman political history incurs both thematic deductions; the narrative ends with Julian in 363. https://www.hachetteindia.com/Home/bookdetails/Info/9781846683701/imperial-triumph

The Precarious Balance|1948|0|10|1945|7,9,8,8,8,9,8,9,8,8|Ludwig Dehio|Models European power struggles through bids for hegemony and resistance from maritime or peripheral powers. The geographic framework is transferable but compresses national differences and economic detail. German original 1948 is verified; later English translation does not reset age. https://ci.nii.ac.jp/ncid/BC04126552?codeamplib=oclc&l=en&linkamp=library-library-filter

Moral Origins|2012|0|0||7,8,7,8,7,8,5,9,8,8|Christopher Boehm|Explores how cooperation, social sanctions and group regulation could shape moral behavior. Ethnographic comparisons give mechanisms to test, but reconstruction of prehistoric selection is indirect. Distinctions among altruism, conformity and punishment add learning without making the evolutionary story certain. https://search.worldcat.org/title/moral-origins-the-evolution-of-virtue-altruism-and-shame/oclc/792684676

Society Against the State|1974|0|10||6,7,7,7,7,8,6,9,7,8|Pierre Clastres|Ethnographic essays argue that some societies actively prevent concentrated coercive authority. The distinction between absence of a state and resistance to state formation is useful. Broad generalization from selected cases and interpretive framing limit evidential confidence. Institutional criticism alone is not extremist advocacy. https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctv1595m3p

The Creation of Inequality|2012|0|10||8,9,8,8,8,9,7,10,8,8|Kent Flannery; Joyce Marcus|Compares how social distinctions become durable rank, inherited privilege and centralized authority. Archaeological variation challenges single-factor stories based only on surplus or population. Substantial cases provide different constraints; slavery is one outcome rather than the predominant historical subject. https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctt2jbvjr

The Evolution of Civilizations|1961|0|10||6,9,8,8,7,8,7,8,7,8|Carroll Quigley|Proposes stages of civilizational expansion and institutional decline. The distinction between productive instruments and self-serving institutions offers a reusable diagnostic question. Large abstractions and flexible retrospective classification weaken testing; read as a comparative model rather than an established law.

A Study of History|1934|0|10||6,9,7,7,6,8,6,10,7,8|Arnold J. Toynbee|A large comparative history organized around civilizational challenge and response. Its breadth supplies historical comparisons, but elastic categories and repeated interpretive schemes lower evidential and density estimates. Religious interpretations require caution; this assessment does not treat the historical series as devotional instruction. Series year is its first volume, 1934.

States and Social Revolutions|1979|0|10||9,9,9,9,8,9,8,10,7,8|Theda Skocpol|Compares France, Russia and China to explain revolution through state structures, international pressures and class relations. Contrasting cases provide strong causal structure with limits from a small selected sample. Historical political explanation is not advocacy of revolution.

Rulers, Religion, and Riches|2017|0|10||8,9,8,8,8,9,8,9,8,8|Jared Rubin|Explains how rulers' sources of legitimacy affect economic and institutional change. Comparisons across Europe and the Middle East make the mechanism transferable, while the prominence assigned to religion needs comparison with alternative causes. Analytical religion does not trigger V5.

The Crisis of Parliamentary Democracy|1923|0|10||5,7,6,6,8,8,6,9,7,8|Carl Schmitt|Distinguishes liberal discussion from democratic identity and examines the weakening of parliamentary justification. The 1926 preface makes exclusionary homogeneity a requirement and treats forced Greek removal from Turkey as an example. V5 is based on that substantive prescription, not the author's later affiliation. Counterfactual evidence and utility retain this flaw. Directly inspected preface, printed pages 9–11; whole-book density remains low-confidence. https://presencial.moodle.ufsc.br/pluginfile.php/1619059/mod_resource/content/0/Schmitt,%20carl.%20The%20Crisis%20of%20Parliamentary%20Democracy.pdf
